count-all-digits-of-a-number.hint: What happens to a number when you divide it by 10? Count how many times you can do that before it runs out. Watch out for n = 0.

factorial-of-a-given-number-i.hint: n! multiplies every whole number from 1 up to n. What should the product start at so that 0! works too?

divisors-of-a-number.hint: Divisors come in pairs: if d divides n, so does n / d. Do you really need to try every number up to n?

Person 0 knows nobody and is known by 1 and 2.

next-greater-element.hint: Scan from the right and keep a stack of candidates. Which candidates can never be an answer again?
why: 1 → 3; 3 → 4; 2 → 4; nothing is greater than 4 to its right.
6 → 8; 0 → 1; 1 → 3; 8 and 3 have nothing greater to the right.
The values only go down.

next-smaller-element.hint: Mirror of next greater: a monotonic stack from the right, this time keeping smaller values.
why: 4 → 2; 8 → 5; 5 → 2; 2 and 25 have nothing smaller to the right.
The values only go up.
Both 5s see 3 next; 3 has nothing after it.

stock-span-problem.hint: For each day you need the nearest earlier day with a higher price. A stack of days can find it fast.
why: For 110: 110, 90, 80, 60, 100 are all ≤ 110, but 120 is not: span 5.
Every price is higher than all before it.
The second 5 covers both 5s; 4 covers only itself.

fractional-knapsack.hint: Which item gives you the most value per unit of weight? Fill the bag in that order, splitting the last item if needed.
why: Take items 1 and 2 whole (160), then 20 of item 3's 30 weight (80).
Only a third of the item fits: 500 × 10 / 30.
Both items fit whole.

shortest-job-first.hint: Each job waits for the total time of the jobs that ran before it. In what order should they run to keep that small?
why: Order 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 gives waits 0, 1, 3, 6, 10; the average is 4.
Waits 0, 1, 3, 6; the average 2.5 rounds down to 2.
A single job never waits.

job-sequencing-problem.hint: Consider the most profitable jobs first and put each one in the latest free slot before its deadline.
why: Job 3 (40) at time 1 and job 1 (20) by time 4.
Jobs 1 (100) and 3 (27) use both time slots.
One job, one slot.

minimum-number-of-bracket-reversals-to-m.hint: First cancel every matched pair. What is left looks like some ')' followed by some '('. How many flips does that need?
why: Matched pairs cancel, leaving ")(((": one ) and three ( that take 3 flips.
Flip the first ) and the last ( to get "()()".
An odd number of brackets can never balance.

n-meetings-in-one-room.hint: To fit the most meetings, which meeting should you pick first: the one that starts earliest, or the one that ends earliest?
why: Meetings ending at 2, 4, 7 and 9 fit one after another.
Every meeting overlaps the others.
There is only one meeting.

minimum-number-of-platforms-required-for.hint: Sort arrivals and departures separately and sweep through time, counting trains in the station.
why: Between 950 and 1100 three trains are in the station.
The first train leaves before the second arrives.
One leaves at 1000 just as the other arrives, so both need a platform.

pre,-post,-inorder-in-one-traversal.hint: Push (node, state) pairs. Each time you see a node, bump its state: the state tells you which order list it belongs to now.
why: The three standard orders of the same tree.
Root 1 with children 2 and 3.
4 has a right child 5, whose left child is 6.

top-view-of-bt.hint: Give each node a horizontal distance (left −1, right +1) and do a level-order walk. Which node per distance is visible from above?
why: The leftmost 4, then 2, 1, 3 and the rightmost 7.
4 and 5 are hidden behind 1 and 3; 6 sticks out to the right.
A single node.

bottom-view-of-bt.hint: Same horizontal distances as top view, but now a later node at the same distance replaces an earlier one.
why: Seen from below: 5, then 10 under 8, 3 under 20, 14 under 22, and 25.
6 is deeper than 1 and 5 at distance 0 and comes later in level order.
1 at distance 0 and 2 at distance 1.

children-sum-property-in-binary-tree.hint: Check each non-leaf node against its children, then check the subtrees the same way.
why: 1 is not 4 + 3.
5 is not 3 + 0.

print-root-to-leaf-path-in-bt.hint: Carry the current path down the recursion. At a leaf, save a copy; on the way back up, remove the last node.
why: The two leaves are 5 and 4.
The leaves are 4, 5 and 3.
The root is also a leaf.

minimum-time-taken-to-burn-the-bt-from-a.hint: Fire can also move up to the parent. First record every node's parent, then spread outward level by level from the target.
why: From 1: 2 and 3 burn at 1 s, 4, 5, 6 at 2 s, 7 at 3 s.
From 7 the fire climbs 4, 2, 1, then down 3, and 5 and 6 burn last at 5 s.
From 3: 1 burns at 1 s, 2 at 2 s.

requirements-needed-to-construct-a-uniqu.hint: Inorder tells you what is left and right of a root; preorder or postorder tell you which node is the root.
why: Preorder gives roots and inorder splits left from right.
Without inorder, a node with one child could be a left or a right child.
The same traversal twice adds no information.

minimum-and-maximum-in-bst.hint: In a BST, smaller values are always to the left. Where does the smallest one live?
why: The leftmost node is 1 and the rightmost is 14.
5 has no left child; 9 is the rightmost.
One node is both.

floor-and-ceil-in-a-bst.hint: Walk down from the root once. Every node you pass is a candidate for floor or ceil depending on its side of key.
why: 10 is the largest value ≤ 11 and 12 the smallest ≥ 11.
6 is in the tree.
Nothing is ≤ 1, and 2 is the smallest value.

kth-smallest-and-largest-element-in-bst.hint: An inorder walk visits BST values in sorted order. Do you need to store them all?
why: Sorted values 1, 2, 3, 4: first and last.
Sorted values 1 to 6: the 3rd from the start is 3, the 3rd from the end is 4.
One node.

inorder-successor-and-predecessor-in-bst.hint: Use the BST ordering while walking down from the root, remembering the last node you passed on each side.
why: Sorted order 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 10, 12: 7 is before 10 and 12 after.
1 is the smallest, so it has no predecessor.
12 is the largest, so it has no successor.

implement-min-heap.hint: Store the tree in an array: children of i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. After a change, sift up or sift down to fix the order.
why: After removing 1 the heap holds 4 and 10; changing 4 to 16 leaves 10 as the minimum.
After removing the only value the heap is empty.
One 3 is removed; the other 3 is still the minimum and two values remain.

implement-max-heap.hint: Same array layout as a min-heap, with the comparison flipped: a parent must be at least as large as its children.
why: After removing 10 the heap holds 4 and 1; changing 4 to 16 makes 16 the maximum.
After removing the only value the heap is empty.
7 is removed; a 3 is the new maximum and two values remain.

heapify-algorithm.hint: Compare the new value with its parent. If it is smaller, move it up; otherwise compare it with its smaller child and move it down.
why: 2 is smaller than its parent 5, so they swap; 2 is not smaller than 1, so it stops.
10 sinks below 3, then below 8.
0 is smaller than its parent 1, so they swap.

build-heap-from-a-given-array.hint: Leaves are already heaps. Start at the last parent and sift each node down, moving toward the root.
why: 5 and 1 swap, then 6 sinks past 1 and 5.
9 and 8 sink below the smaller children.
Already a min-heap.

check-if-an-array-represents-a-min-heap-.hint: Only parents need checking. Which indices have at least one child?
why: 20 has the child 15, which is smaller.
Equal values are allowed.

convert-min-heap-to-max-heap.hint: You can ignore the fact that it is a min-heap: build a max-heap from the array bottom-up.
why: The largest value 30 rises to the root.
3 rises to the root.
Each parent ends up at least as large as its children.

heap-sort.hint: With a max-heap, the largest value is at index 0. Swap it to the end, shrink the heap, and fix the root.
why: The values in increasing order.
The duplicate 5s stay together.
Negative values sort first.

sort-a-k-sorted-array.hint: The smallest remaining value must be among the next k + 1 elements. Keep just those in a min-heap.
why: Every value is at most 2 places from its spot.
Every value is at most 3 places from its spot.
Neighbouring pairs swap.

maximum-sum-combination.hint: Sort both arrays. The biggest sum pairs the two largest values; the next candidates are neighbours of the pair you just used. A max-heap and a visited set help.

traversal-techniques.hint: DFS goes deep before wide (recursion or a stack); BFS goes level by level with a queue. Mark vertices visited when you add them.
why: DFS reaches 3 through 1 before going to 2; BFS visits 0's neighbours 1 and 2 first.
DFS walks around the square; BFS reaches 1 and 3 before 2.
2 is the only neighbour of 0, and 1 hangs off 2.

detect-a-cycle-in-an-undirected-graph.hint: During BFS or DFS, reaching an already visited vertex that is not the one you came from means a cycle. Check every component.
why: 0 → 1 → 4 → 3 → 0 is a loop.
The graph is a straight line 0 - 1 - 2 - 3.
2, 3 and 4 form a triangle.

topological-sort-or-kahns-algorithm.hint: Count incoming edges for every vertex. Vertices with none can go first; removing them frees others.
why: 4 and 5 have no incoming edges, so they start the order.
0 must come before 1 and 2, which come before 3.
The edges point 2 → 1 → 0.

detect-a-cycle-in-a-directed-graph.hint: In DFS, track which vertices are on the current path. Meeting one of those again means a cycle.
why: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 1 is a loop.
0 reaches 3 two ways, but you never come back to where you started.

shortest-path-in-undirected-graph-with-u.hint: When every edge costs the same, the first time BFS reaches a vertex is the shortest way there.
why: For example 6 is reached as 0 → 1 → 2 → 6 in 3 steps.
3 has no edge, so it cannot be reached.
0 has a direct edge to both 1 and 2.

shortest-path-with-minimum-effort.hint: Each move costs 1, so think BFS from the source over open cells.
why: A path of 3 moves exists from (0, 1) to (2, 2).
The bottom-right cell is walled off by zeros.
Down, then right.

shortest-path-in-dag.hint: In a DAG you can process vertices in topological order and relax each one's outgoing edges exactly once.
why: 0 reaches 1 at cost 2 and 2 at cost 1; nothing reaches 3.
3 is reached most cheaply through 4 → 5 → 3: 1 + 4 + 1 = 6.
No edge leaves 0.

dijkstra's-algorithm.hint: Always settle the unvisited vertex with the smallest known distance next. A priority queue makes that fast.
why: The only edge costs 9.
From 2: 1 costs 3, and 0 is cheaper through 1 (3 + 1) than directly (6).
No edge reaches 2.

print-shortest-path-.hint: Run Dijkstra and remember, for each vertex, which vertex you reached it from. Walk those links back from n.
why: 1 → 4 → 3 → 5 costs 1 + 3 + 1 = 5, cheaper than through 2.
Going through 2 costs 2; the direct edge costs 5.
No edge reaches 3.

minimum-multiplications-to-reach-end.hint: Each value 0..99999 is a node and each multiplication is an edge of cost 1. That is a shortest-path problem.
why: Four multiplications are the fewest that reach 66175.
Multiplying 1 by 2s and 4s never gives an odd number above 1.

bellman-ford-algorithm.hint: Relax every edge V - 1 times. If one more round still improves something, there is a negative cycle.
why: For example 4 is cheapest via 0 → 1 → 5 → 3 → 4: 5 - 3 + 1 - 2 = 1.
From 1: 2 costs 3, and 0 costs 3 - 2 = 1; nothing reaches 3.
1 → 2 → 1 adds up to -1, so distances can drop forever.

floyd-warshall-algorithm.hint: Allow one more intermediate vertex at a time and check whether going through it is shorter.
why: For example 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 costs 2 + 3 + 1 = 6.
0 → 1 → 2 (7) beats the direct 43.
No edges between the two vertices.

disjoint-set-.hint: Every set has a representative. find follows parent links to it; path compression and union by rank or size keep the trees short.
why: 0 and 1 were joined; 3 was only joined with 2.
0 - 1 - 2 are joined; 3 is alone.
Nothing is joined at first; after the union, 1 and 0 share a set.

find-the-mst-weight.hint: Kruskal: take edges from cheapest up, skipping any that would close a cycle. Or Prim: grow the tree from one vertex with a heap.
why: Edges 1, 2 and 3 connect all four vertices; the 4 would close a cycle.
Edges 1 and 3 connect everything.
Only one edge.

kosaraju's-algorithm.hint: Do a DFS and record finishing order. Then reverse every edge and run DFS again in reverse finishing order; each new DFS tree is one component.
why: {0, 1, 2} form a loop; 3 and 4 are on their own.
0 → 1 → 2 → 0 is one loop.
A chain with no way back: every vertex is its own component.

articulation-point-in-graph.hint: Track discovery times and the lowest time reachable from each subtree. A child that cannot reach above its parent makes the parent a cut vertex.
why: Removing 0 cuts off 1; removing 2 cuts off 4, 5 and 6.
Removing either middle vertex splits the path.
A triangle stays connected whatever single vertex you remove.

frog-jump.hint: The cheapest way to reach stair i comes from stair i - 1 or i - 2. Build up from stair 0.

frog-jump-with-k-distances.hint: Same idea as Frog Jump, but stair i can be reached from any of the k stairs before it.
why: The cheapest route, trying jumps of up to 4 each time, totals 40.

ninja's-training.hint: The best total up to a day depends on which activity you did last. Keep the best score for each last activity.
why: 70 + 50 + 90: activity 3, then 2, then 3 again (not consecutive).
70 + 20 + 200 beats taking 180 on day 2.

subset-sum-equals-to-target.hint: For each element and each remaining target, either use the element or skip it. Memoise on (index, target).
why: The possible sums are 2, 3, 5, 7, 8 and 10.

count-subsets-with-sum-k.hint: Like subset sum, but count the ways from both choices. Be careful with zeros in the base case.
why: {1, 2}, {1, the other 2} and {3}.
Either 1, each with or without the 0.

count-partitions-with-given-difference.hint: If S1 - S2 = diff and S1 + S2 = total, then S2 is fixed. Count subsets with that sum.
why: S2 must be 3: {1, 2}, {other 1, 2} and {3}.
S2 must be 7: only {5, 2}.
The total is 3, so a difference of 4 is impossible.

0-and-1-knapsack.hint: For each item and each capacity, compare taking it (if it fits) with leaving it.
why: Items 2 and 3 weigh 50 and give 220.
Items 2 and 4 weigh 7 and give 90.
The only item is too heavy.

unbounded-knapsack.hint: Like 0/1 knapsack, but after taking an item you stay on the same item, since it can be taken again.
why: Two of item 2 and one of item 1: 11 + 11 + 5, weight 10.
Items of weight 3 and 5: 40 + 70.
The only item is too heavy.

rod-cutting-problem.hint: This is unbounded knapsack in disguise: piece lengths are weights and prices are values.
why: A piece of 2 (6) and a piece of 6 (19).
Eight pieces of length 1 at 3 each.
One piece of length 2 is worth more than two of length 1.

longest-common-substring.hint: Let dp[i][j] be the length of a common run ending at str1[i] and str2[j]. A mismatch resets it.
why: "ab" is in both.
"abcd" is in both.
No letter is shared.

count-palindromic-subsequences.hint: Count for every range [i, j]. When the end characters match, the pairs inside can be wrapped by them.
why: Only the four single letters.
a, a, b, and "aa".
Three single a's, three "aa" pairs, and "aaa".

print-longest-increasing-subsequence.hint: Compute the LIS length ending at each index, and remember the previous index that gave it. Follow those links back.
why: Six values, each larger than the last.
Both 1, 3, 4 and 1, 2, 4 have length 3; 1, 3, 4 uses earlier indices.
The values only go down, so any single value is an LIS.

longest-bitonic-subsequence.hint: Compute the longest increasing run ending at each index from the left, and the longest decreasing run starting there from the right.
why: 1, 2, 3, 6, 8 rising, then 7.
Increasing only; the decreasing part is empty.

matrix-chain-multiplication.hint: Try every place to make the last split, and take the cheapest. Memoise on the range of matrices.
why: Multiplying left to right costs 6000 + 12000 + 20000.
Two matrices: 4 × 2 × 3.
((AB)C)D costs 6 + 12 + 12.

different-ways-to-evaluate-a-boolean-exp.hint: For every range, count the ways it can be true and the ways it can be false. Split at each operator and combine the counts.
why: Four of the five bracketings come out true.
(T^F)|F and T^(F|F) are both true.
F & anything is false.
